lesson.title: The Traffic Law of Circuits: Kirchhoff's Current Law
lesson.summary: Kirchhoff's Current Law says charge cannot pile up at a junction, so every bit of current flowing into a node must flow back out. It turns a tangled web of wires into a solvable system of equations.
lesson.body:
Imagine a highway interchange where cars merge and split but none of them vanish or appear out of nowhere. Every car that enters the interchange eventually leaves it. Kirchhoff's Current Law, or KCL, says the same thing about electric charge at a node, the point where two or more branches of a circuit meet. The sum of the currents flowing into a node must equal the sum of the currents flowing out. Written as an algebraic sum with entering currents positive and leaving currents negative, KCL simply states that the total is zero at every node, at every instant.

The reason this law holds is conservation of charge, one of the most reliable facts in physics. A node is just a junction of wires, it has no room to store electric charge under normal DC conditions. If more charge arrived than left, that charge would have to accumulate somewhere inside the node, and since current is defined as charge per unit time, an imbalance would mean charge is being created or destroyed, which never happens. So KCL is not an approximation or a rule of thumb, it is a direct consequence of the definition of current and the fact that charge is conserved.

KCL is what makes parallel circuits behave the way they do. When a single source feeds several parallel branches, the current from the source splits among them, but the pieces must always add back up to the original total at the node where the branches meet. This is the mathematical backbone behind the idea that parallel resistors share current in proportion to their conductance, and it is also the tool you use to find an unknown branch current when you already know the others.

Consider a 12 volt source connected to two resistors in parallel, a 4 ohm resistor and a 6 ohm resistor, joined at a common node. Each branch obeys Ohm's law independently because both resistors see the full 12 volts. The current through the 4 ohm branch is 12 divided by 4, which is 3 amps. The current through the 6 ohm branch is 12 divided by 6, which is 2 amps. KCL says the current leaving the source into that node must equal 3 amps plus 2 amps, or 5 amps total. Check it against the equivalent parallel resistance: 4 times 6 divided by the sum of 4 and 6 gives 24 divided by 10, or 2.4 ohms, and 12 volts divided by 2.4 ohms is exactly 5 amps. The two methods agree because they describe the same physical fact from two directions.

KCL earns its place alongside Kirchhoff's Voltage Law as one of the two pillars of circuit analysis. Every systematic technique for solving circuits with many nodes and branches, including nodal analysis, is really just KCL applied at every node and then solved as a system of equations. Beyond the math, KCL has very practical consequences: it is why a fuse or breaker rated for a certain current must account for every parallel path feeding a junction, and why wires feeding a splitter need to be sized for the sum of what leaves it, not just one branch.
